## BOOK ONE.

In an age far removed from our own, and the era of which would be very difficult for us to pinpoint—since no historical text or chronological record can assist us in determining it—the Kingdom of Epirus <note>A coastal region in northwestern Greece and southern Albania, frequently featured as a site of high adventure in chivalric romance.</note> was ruled by a Prince named Alicant. This King traced his lineage back to Pyrrhus, the son of the valiant Achilles <note>Pyrrhus, also known as Neoptolemus, was a legendary Greek hero of the Trojan War; by claiming this descent, the author gives the King a prestigious "epic" pedigree.</note>. ## OF THE SUN. Book I.

...marched throughout the entire day, they stopped towards evening in a woods where they resolved to spend the night, after having consumed a portion of the provisions they had brought with them. Trébatius <note>The protagonist, also known as the Knight of the Sun.</note> moved a little away from his small troop and lay down near a tree, fully armed, having his horse near him, which he had stripped of its harness only as much as was necessary to allow it to graze; he fell asleep peacefully, dreaming, however, always of the happiness he had tasted the day before, and of which he had been almost immediately deprived. 

At the break of day, his sleep was interrupted by cries and moans which appeared to him to be those of a woman: the Emperor could not be indifferent to the tears of that weak and lovely sex <note>A common 18th-century chivalric phrasing referring to women as the "fairer sex" deserving of protection.</note>, whose kindness he had just experienced. ### OF THE SUN. Book I.

At the end of this glorious campaign, the wise Lirgandé <note>Lirgandé is a powerful enchanter and mentor figure in this cycle of chivalric romances, similar to Merlin in Arthurian legend.</note>, having called the Knight of the Sun to his side, said to him: “Prince, you have just accomplished the first of the great and glorious enterprises by which you must illustrate the course of your life. You alone and the lovely Claberinde <note>Claberinde is a warrior princess and companion-in-arms to the Knight.</note> could have achieved it. Now, it is time for you to concern yourself with matters that are more personal. You are ignorant of who your parents are, and you shall only know them when you are in the very place of your birth, of which you have only a confused memory. A thousand obstacles and countless perils will oppose this discovery <term>reconnoissance: the formal "recognition" or revelation of a hero's true identity and noble lineage, a common trope in romance literature</term>, but your courage and your wisdom will not fail you in these troubling circumstances. Furthermore, I shall watch over you; I will fly to your aid, and my art <note>original: "mon art"; referring here to his magical powers and prophetic foresight</note> will serve you in the most difficult of situations.”

The young Knight, after having thanked him and embraced his knees <note>a traditional gesture of deep reverence, gratitude, or supplication dating back to antiquity</note>, asked him in vain and on several occasions which way he should turn his steps. He could draw from the Enchanter only these words: “Entrust yourself to your destiny.”

Rodarant, seeing no one appear the day after the capture of Rosiclair, sent to ask insolently at the Court of Constantinople if all the Greek Knighthood had renounced fighting him. This audacious remark indignant Prince Claberinde; he flew to punish its author, but he, like the others, was caught in the net. Finally, the great Trebatius <note>The Emperor of Constantinople and father of the main heroes.</note>, as surprised as he was irritated by the loss of so many illustrious Knights, decided to march out himself to go and deliver them: he advanced proudly and made himself known to Rodarant. ## THE KNIGHT

Having recognized the voice of **Claridiane**, his inner turmoil caused such a violent shock <note>original: "révolution" — in 18th-century medical and psychological terms, this refers to a sudden, overwhelming physical or emotional upheaval.</note> within him that he fell unconscious upon his horse. They rushed to his aid and carried him into the Palace, where the physicians, after employing all their art to restore him to life and health, left him alone with his faithful Squires <note>original: "Ecuyers" — noble attendants who served a knight and cared for his equipment.</note>. Having come to himself again, recalling the words of his Lady, and judging the weight of her anger, he gave himself up to the most cruel despair. Far from waiting for her to fight her or to justify himself, he resolved to depart before the break of day; he could not forgive himself for having been on the verge of shedding such precious blood, and for having employed against her the strength and the sword that his heart intended for her defense. He had himself armed and left **Constantinople**, mounted upon his good horse **Cornelin**, always followed by his Squires, who, despite his orders, would not abandon him. His intention was, if he could not find death, to hide himself henceforth from all eyes, to no longer appear before his Lady, and to renounce all manner of knightly exploits. This generous conduct placed the English Monarch <note>King Oliver, who had been leading an invasion of the Greek Empire.</note> in a great dilemma; on one hand, he recognized that he owed a profound debt of gratitude to the Emperor Trebatius and to Rosiclair: on the other, he believed it his duty to avenge the death of his son Theodoart, and the abduction of his daughter Olive. He decided to order his troops to suspend all acts of hostility against the Greeks.

As for Rosiclair, he received in Constantinople all the congratulations that were his due, as well as the thanks of the beautiful Olive for his noble behavior toward her father; she hoped that these actions would disarm the King of Great Britain.

Alicandre was not long in learning that he had made a cruel mistake. To appear fully settled in the new Arcadia, and to count himself among Carline's subjects, the man calling himself Philidor bought a rustic hut in the hamlet where she lived, along with a fairly large flock. It was the inheritance of an old Shepherd, who had recently died without children. At the same time, he took into his service the good man’s farmhands and maidservants, who were perfectly skilled in rural economy <term>rural economy: the management of farm resources and livestock</term>. He specifically declared to them that he would let them keep all the profits they might earn, provided that his sheep were the finest and best-kept in the region, and that they had the good fortune of pleasing Carline.

Upon entering this country dwelling, he found it furnished with the cleanest and most convenient furniture, though suited to the lifestyle he intended to embrace. In a kind of small dressing room, or partitioned space within the hut, he saw with surprise his weapons, set aside for the occasion when he might need them—and especially his good sword. The faithful squire Fidelio presented himself to him, dressed as a simple shepherd like his master. One of them, who was very resentful, resolved to take revenge in a way that was most distressing for the subjects of King Benin <note>The name Benin is derived from the French word "bénin," meaning kind, gentle, or harmless.</note> (this was the name of the father of the Princess, who was called Suffisante <note>In French, "Suffisante" means self-sufficient, but in this context, it carries the negative connotation of being conceited or stuck-up.</note>). 

The wicked Fairy thus performed a terrible enchantment which resulted in a frightful monster that began to ravage all of King Benin’s country, destroying the harvests, burning the houses, and eating the women and small children. They consulted the oracle <note>In ancient stories, an oracle was a priest or priestess acting as a medium through whom advice or prophecy was sought from the gods.</note> on the manner of delivering themselves from this scourge. It replied that there was no other way than to surrender to the dragon the most beautiful young lady of the Kingdom, and this was, without contradiction, the Princess, the King’s daughter. 

One can well imagine that the Court was in the greatest consternation; but as the devastation continued, and the oracle always said the same thing, they were finally forced to submit. King Benin and Queen Benine, with tears in their eyes, led their daughter into a valley at the bottom of which was the cavern that served as a retreat for the monster. The slayer of heads finally destroyed them all, and finished killing the monster by driving his sword into its heart. He then wanted to take the heads and preserve them as monuments of his victory, but they were too numerous and most of them too large for him to be able to carry them. He contented himself, therefore, with tearing out the tongues from all these heads, and he gathered them in a small bag that had originally served him for carrying some provisions. He was about to leave the valley when his faithful greyhound <term>lévrier <note>A "lévrier" is a sighthound or greyhound; in French fairy tales, these dogs often possess near-human intelligence.</note></term> began to gather garlands of green grass, and having made a pile of them, showed it to his master to encourage him to take it as well. Felicio did not understand why his dog was making this—if one may put it this way—proposal to him; then the clever greyhound began to bite and tear one of these heads in two with its teeth, and after going to find some leaves of the grass he had gathered, he applied them to the parts that had been separated, and instantly they were found perfectly joined. prominent Lord <note>original: "considérable." "Sire," he said, addressing the good King, "it is I who killed the monster that was ravaging your lands and sought to devour your daughter; and these sixty heads that I bring are the proof of it." 

It was difficult to counter such an argument; thus, everyone was inclined to believe him. As he asked for the hand of the Princess whom he claimed to have saved, it was felt that it could not be refused to him. It was true, however, that he had only passed through the valley moments after Felicio had left, after the Princess had fled, and he had only had the trouble of picking up the heads cut off by another. 

But in the end, no one could contradict him, not even Suffisante <note>The name of the Princess.</note>, even though she was in despair at the thought of marrying him. Preparations for their wedding were already underway, and arrangements were being made to hold magnificent festivals for the occasion, when Felicio was informed of it. It was only then that he learned that she was the reward intended for the victor of the monster.

# VIRELAY <term>Virelay: A form of old French verse, usually intended to be set to music, characterized by a specific rhyme scheme and a recurring refrain.</term>

I am more satisfied than a King,
Without trouble, pomp, or misery;
My sheep and my dog are mine,
And I, I belong to my Shepherdess.

---

From the break of day upon the plain,
My flock leaps under my rule;
In the evening, if I find my Queen,
I am more satisfied than a King.

---

We take our meals in the cool air,
Cheerfulness is worth more than fine dining; <note>original: "bonne chere" — refers to the pleasure of the table and high-quality food.</note>
We eat nothing but fruit, but
Without trouble, pomp, or misery.

---

For the great ones, we feel little envy;
Their appearance alone causes dread;

I am more satisfied than a King,

My sheep, my dog are mine,

I am more satisfied than a King.

---

Their very appearance causes dread;
I have neither castle nor lordship,
My sheep, my dog are mine.

It was thus that by storytelling, singing, and loving, Claridian, under the name of Filidor, spent an entire year in the new Arcadia <note>Arcadia is a legendary Greek province celebrated in literature as an idyllic, pastoral paradise of shepherds and simple living.</note>. It was only at the end of this time that his happiness was disturbed by the jealousy of a disguised Prince, who, like our hero, had left his palace and his status as a Knight to come occupy a hut in the domain and under the laws of Carline. His true name was Polismarque, Prince of Damascus; he had taken, within the hamlet, the name of the shepherd Polimere. Desperate to see that Filidor was preferred over him, although the favors this lover obtained were very slight, he resolved to take his revenge. His weapons were hidden at the back of his hut; he took them up again in secret, and with the help of some men he had gathered, he had the audacity to enter the peaceful retreat of the beautiful Carline and to carry her off at daybreak. Fortunately, while passing in front of Filidor’s dwelling, her cries woke him. The return of the Knight of the Sun <note>The "Knight of the Sun" (Chevalier du Soleil) is the titular hero of this 16th-century Spanish romance (originally *Espejo de Príncipes y Caballeros*), which became a massive hit in French and English translations.</note> to Constantinople, and his reunion with Claridian <note>The French text uses "Claridiane." The triumph of Elene <note>Elene: A variant name used in this French translation for the hero of the romance, known in English and Spanish traditions as the Knight of the Sun.</note> led the beautiful Princess of Rome to conceive the hope of being united to the victor, when a marvelous and divine voice was heard in the public square of the ancient Capital of the world, and announced that the conqueror of the Giants and the Princes of Gabinia <note>Gabinia: A fictional kingdom or region, likely derived from the ancient city of Gabii near Rome, often used in chivalric romances to provide exotic origins for villainous characters.</note> was worthy to attempt the adventure of the monument of Brutus, and to win the armor and the sword of this last of the Romans.

The monument of Brutus was situated at one end of the City, atop one of the seven hills of Rome; it was a small ancient Temple, in the form of a rotunda, which had been erected—precisely when is not known—to the glory of the last defender of Roman liberty. In the midst of several columns of jasper, porphyry, and alabaster, one could see the statue of Brutus in white marble, dressed in brilliant armor of polished and gilded steel; a superb sword was part of the set. But instead of being in its scabbard, attached to the statue's side, it was plunged into the heart of the Hero, who had killed himself after having lost the battle of Philippi <note>battle of Philippi: Fought in 42 BCE, this was the final battle between the forces of Mark Antony and Octavian (Caesar Augustus) and the forces of Brutus and Cassius, who had assassinated Julius Caesar. Brutus committed suicide after his defeat.</note> against Caesar Augustus.

The text describes a rotunda temple on a Roman hill containing a marble statue of Brutus, whose sword is eternally plunged into his own chest.</summary>

The adventure was too grand for the Prince of the Dacians <note>Dacians: An ancient people from the region of modern-day Romania; in chivalric romance, they are often depicted as noble and formidable warriors.</note> to refuse the attempt; far from seeking to prevent him, the Emperor and Roselie felt that after seeing it through to the end, the victor would be all the more worthy of their alliance. 

The day was thus set for this brilliant expedition: the playful Arbolinde laughingly told Elene that since he was going to win such a beautiful sword, he had no need of his own, and she asked him for it. The Prince, ever gallant without being in love <note>The text notes that Elene is courteous to all women but his heart remains elsewhere, a common trait for the hero of a "romance of chivalry."</note>, willingly surrendered it to her; and the next day, ascending the hill in full view of all Rome, he advanced toward the Temple. 

As soon as he drew near, an enormous serpent emerged. The Knight, who had no sword, was content to oppose its fury with his shield until, seizing it in his arms, he strangled it, just as Hercules had once done when fighting similar monsters <note>original: "Hercule"; a reference to the Greek hero's many labors involving serpents and hydras, emphasizing Elene’s semi-divine strength.</note>.

Rosemonde—troubled on one hand by his actions, and softened on the other by the Knight's protestations—forgot that she had a brother to avenge, and felt instead all the merit of the repentance shown by his killer, and the value of the tenderness he swore to her.

At the same time, the Princess saw rise, through magical power, an alabaster <note>Alabaster is a fine-grained, translucent stone, often white or veined, used in the ancient and medieval world for precious ornaments and tombs because of its smooth, ethereal glow.</note> pyramid that covered the body of her unfortunate brother. An inscription was engraved there in gold letters, written in verse and addressed to the King of Chalcedon <note>Chalcedon was an ancient maritime city in Asia Minor; in the context of this romance, it represents a distant and noble kingdom.</note>: here are the words:

> Unfortunate monarch, you lose on the same day
> Your young son and your lovely daughter:
> But you will see repaired by love
> The ills that Mars <note>original: "Mars"; the Roman god of war, here used as a metaphor for the combat and violence that claimed the Prince's life.</note> has done to your family.

This monument and this mysterious, magical epitaph <term>a short text written in memory of a deceased person, typically inscribed on a tomb</term>, which seemed to announce that Rosemonde and her young brother were enclosed in the same tomb, produced exactly the effect one might expect. The following day, there was great anxiety regarding the fate of the Prince and the Princess; they were sought for a long time to no avail. Finally, the monument was discovered, though no one could guess who had raised it, nor how the brother and sister had lost their lives. The King, their father, wept for them bitterly; but he was eventually consoled, grounding himself in the hope that had been given to him through supernatural means.

### THE KNIGHT

The Enchanter flew away on his cloud and betook himself to the island which belonged to him, and which was called the secret island. It was there that Sélage was raising the five children whom he intended to one day be the ministers of his vengeance <note>In chivalric romances, "ministers of vengeance" refers to characters raised specifically to carry out a vendetta, often against their own kin</note>; the first of these were the son and the daughter to whom Floralinde had given birth in her prison, and the three others were Torinian, Prince of Persia (son of Brandicel and Clarinée), Argante, Prince of Phoenicia, and Clariel, Prince of Assyria. We shall learn in the following Book what was the fate of these five children destined for the greatest adventures.

Meanwhile, the Enchanter having left the forbidden island <note>original: "l'isle défendue"</note>, the Princes who remained there were some time in recovering from the turmoil he had cast into their souls; finally, the wise Lirgandé <note>Lirgandé is a recurring "good" magician in this literary cycle, acting as a protector to the heroes, often serving as a foil to the malevolent Sélage</note> appeared and assured them that if he could not destroy the effect of the conjurations of his colleague and enemy, he would at least watch over the consequences that these enchantments might have. He answered them that Brandafidel could remain on the island in all safety, and there watch over the beautiful Floralinde; and that the other Princes and Knights could depart to return either to their own countries or to Greece. Androne was escorting to his own States the Princess of Holland, whom he had just married in France; the son of Trebatius <note>Referring to Rosiclair, whose father Trebatius is the Emperor of Greece in this cycle of stories</note> was charmed by this happy encounter, and desired to render them even greater services, when he was informed that the Corsair he had just defeated was the master of a nearby island in the Archipelago <note>term: "Archipel"; specifically referring to the Aegean Sea between Greece and Turkey, known for its many islands</note>, which he had turned into a den of dangerous Pirates who infested these seas. 

Our Knights did not hesitate to land there; they destroyed this settlement which was harmful to the safety of commerce, and after having drawn from it all the supplies that might be useful to Androne to facilitate his return and that of his Princess to his homeland, they let them continue on their way. Rosabel, having unlaced and removed his helmet, appeared with his face uncovered; it was then that Rosiclair had cause to be struck by the resemblance of his features to those of the beautiful Olive. <note>Olive is a princess and the lover of Rosiclair; she is Rosabel's mother.</note>

> “All that I have known of my birth until now,” Rosabel then said to his illustrious father, “is that a lioness brought me, about fifteen years ago, into the Kingdom of Nicaea <note>original: "Niquée," a fictionalized version of Nicaea common in chivalric romances.</note>, and set me down at the feet of the King of that country. Struck by this kind of miracle, he determined to raise me. I was then about two or three years old. I have since learned that the King had found tablets <note>Small, portable writing surfaces, often made of wood, ivory, or metal, used for important messages.</note> on my person which, though they gave him only slight indications regarding my birth, at least informed him of my name. Here they are; they were only returned to me a few days before my departure from Nicaea.”

At the same time, Rosabel presented these tablets to Rosiclair; they were made of a precious metal and enriched with gemstones. On the first leaf, which opened easily, one could read: “The child to whom these tablets belong...”

While passing again through the islands of the Archipelago <term>Archipelago: a term frequently used in early modern literature to refer specifically to the Aegean Sea between Greece and Turkey.</term>, they touched upon the shore of one of them, where they thought they saw a young woman crying out loudly, calling for help for her mistress, who at that very moment was about to be ravished by a Giant. The Knights immediately thought of coming to her aid, but Rosabel, getting ahead of all the others, said:

Trebatius, the Knight of the Sun—who had been called Emperor Alphebe since he began reigning in Trebizond—and even Claridiane herself, had rushed there upon receiving the news that Claridian was in the forest, sustaining a terrible combat against Brufaldor; that four other Knights were fighting in the same place, and that the illustrious Rosiclair had been recognized among them. ...which is accompanied by a long series of great and noble deeds.

This day was thus once again filled with several of those touching and interesting scenes, of which we have already many times presented the picture. The return of Rosiclair, Claridian, and Archisilore <note>These are the central heroes of the romance: Rosiclair and Claridian (the Knight of the Sun) are brothers and the sons of Emperor Trebatius.</note> to Constantinople, and the recognition of Elene, <note>The "recognition" or reunion of Elene (Helena), daughter of the Knight of the Sun and Empress Claribelle.</note> gave rise to brilliant festivities. Meridian, Oristide, and Rosemonde were present; the young Clarinde of France, son of Claberinde and Lindaraffe, and Bradiman of Persia, son of Brandisel and Clarinée, were also there. We leave it to the following books to take up the continuation of these happy events.

->*End of the First Volume.*<-
